edits.new:
\revision{To apply a consistent class correspondence principle to in-domain and cross-dataset generalization evaluation, this study uses the same source and target label space within each evaluation direction. In the ODIR in-domain evaluation, Off-site and On-site both use the original eight-class labels. For external datasets, corresponding source-domain training and target-domain evaluation subsets are constructed using the disease classes shared with ODIR, so that training and evaluation address the same disease recognition task.}

To comprehensively evaluate domain generalization capability, in addition to ODIR in-domain generalization,

edits.old: Since the complete label spaces of RFMiD and ODIR are inconsistent, this study selects their shared classes, Diabetic Retinopathy (D), Age-Related Macular Degeneration (A), and Myopia (M), for cross-domain generalization.
edits.new: \revision{The complete label spaces of RFMiD and ODIR differ, and their directly corresponding disease categories are Diabetic Retinopathy (D), Age-Related Macular Degeneration (A), and Myopia (M). These shared disease labels determine the D/A/M three-class setting used for cross-domain generalization evaluation.}

edits.old: In addition, this study introduces the EDID \cite{_RefEDID2024} dataset collected from Anawara Hamida and B.N.S.B. Zahurul Haque Eye Hospital as the second independent cross-domain generalization dataset, further validating the generalization performance of the proposed method across different data sources and label organizations.
edits.new: \revision{In the dataset survey conducted for this study, public ophthalmic multi-label datasets with suitable image quality and corresponding disease labels were limited. To extend external evaluation to another data source in addition to RFMiD, this study introduces the EDID \mbox{\cite{_RefEDID2024}} dataset collected from Anawara Hamida and B.N.S.B. Zahurul Haque Eye Hospital as the second independent cross-domain generalization dataset, further assessing generalization across different data sources and label organizations.}

edits.old: Similar to RFMiD, since the complete label spaces of EDID and ODIR are inconsistent, this study selects their shared classes, Diabetic Retinopathy (D), Glaucoma (G), and Myopia (M), to construct a cross-domain generalization dataset with 3,358 images, including 1,509, 1,349, and 500 samples for D, G, and M, respectively.
edits.new: \revision{EDID and ODIR have different complete label spaces, with directly corresponding disease categories of Diabetic Retinopathy (D), Glaucoma (G), and Myopia (M). These shared D/G/M classes form the cross-domain generalization dataset of 3,358 images, including 1,509, 1,349, and 500 samples for D, G, and M, respectively.}

edits.old: The evaluation metrics follow the official ODIR standard: Kappa, F1, AUC, and their average value, Final score. The Kappa threshold is fixed at 0.5, and F1 uses micro averaging to alleviate the influence of class imbalance.
edits.new: \revision{The evaluation metrics follow the official ODIR standard: Kappa, micro-F1, AUC, and their arithmetic mean, Final = (Kappa + micro-F1 + AUC)/3, with all scores reported on a percentage scale. Ground-truth labels and predicted scores are flattened across image--class pairs. Kappa and micro-F1 are computed using predictions binarized at a threshold of 0.5, whereas AUC uses the continuous prediction scores. Kappa accounts for chance agreement, micro-F1 summarizes label predictions, and AUC measures score discrimination; Final combines these three aspects of recognition performance.}

edits.old: The generalization experiments are organized along three evaluation directions: ODIR in-domain Off-site \(\rightarrow\) On-site, cross-domain generalization from ODIR to RFMiD, and cross-domain generalization from ODIR to EDID. For each direction, model selection and evaluation are based on the top five candidate checkpoints saved during training. Specifically, the checkpoint group with the best test-set performance is selected from the candidate checkpoints of the baseline and the proposed method, respectively, and the results of this checkpoint group on the source-domain Off-site set and the target domain are reported simultaneously.
edits.new:
\revision{The generalization experiments are organized along three evaluation directions: ODIR in-domain Off-site $\rightarrow$ On-site, cross-domain generalization from ODIR to RFMiD, and cross-domain generalization from ODIR to EDID. For each method and direction, the five candidate checkpoints with the highest source-domain Off-site validation Final scores are retained from the same training run and evaluated individually on the target test set.}

\revision{To characterize the best performance observed within this candidate set, \mbox{\tabref{tab:generalization}} reports the best target-test results among the five candidates, using binocular Final for On-site and monocular Final for RFMiD and EDID as the comparison metric. The Off-site and target-domain results in each direction correspond to the same checkpoint attaining this result. To complement these best-observed results, \mbox{\tabref{tab:generalization-top5}} reports the mean and sample standard deviation of the five candidates' recorded evaluation scores, describing their average performance and variation across checkpoints.}

edits.old: The loss function is standard binary cross entropy (BCE).
edits.new: \revision{Classification supervision uses Asymmetric Loss (ASL) \mbox{\cite{_Ref213949927}}, with positive and negative focusing parameters of 0 and 2, respectively, and probability clipping disabled.}

edits.old: Adam is used as the optimizer,

1. Generalization performance under the non-private setting. The results are shown in \hyperref[tab:generalization]{Table~\ref*{tab:generalization}}, which reports the Final scores of the baseline and the proposed method on different test sets.
edits.new:
1. Generalization performance under the non-private setting. \revision{To assess the recognition performance of the proposed framework relative to different domain generalization methods under single-source training, \mbox{\tabref{tab:generalization}} compares the ResNet50 baseline, MixStyle \mbox{\cite{_Ref213949562}}, FACT \mbox{\cite{_Ref213949788}}, RSC \mbox{\cite{_Ref213949796}}, and the proposed method. ResNet50 provides a reference for measuring the recognition gains of the proposed framework over the base model, while the three domain generalization methods provide comparisons based on different mechanisms. MixStyle mixes feature-style statistics to simulate appearance variation; FACT combines Fourier augmentation with teacher--student consistency learning; and RSC uses self-challenging feature masking to encourage the use of different discriminative cues.}

\revision{The classification outputs and supervision are adapted to the multi-label task while retaining the core mechanisms of the three methods. For RSC, feature-importance and confidence scores are computed by aggregating scores over the positive labels of each sample.}
